paragraphs.heading: A small world past Neptune
paragraphs.text: Pluto is a dwarf planet. It lies in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies out beyond Neptune's orbit. Like its neighbours there, it is made mostly of ice and rock, and it is far smaller than the inner planets. It has about one-sixth of the Moon's mass and one-third of its volume. Among objects that orbit the Sun directly, it ranks ninth by size and tenth by mass. It is narrowly the biggest known body beyond Neptune by volume, yet Eris, which is denser, outweighs it.

paragraphs.heading: A long, tilted orbit
paragraphs.text: Pluto's orbit is somewhat stretched and tilted, taking it between 30 and 49 astronomical units from the Sun. At a distance of 39.5 AU, sunlight needs 5.5 hours to arrive. At times Pluto swings closer to the Sun than Neptune, but a steady orbital resonance keeps the two from ever colliding. One Pluto year lasts 247.94 Earth years, so it will finish its first full lap since its discovery only in 2178.

paragraphs.heading: Moons and a visit
paragraphs.text: Pluto has five known moons: Charon, Styx, Nix, Kerberos and Hydra. Charon, the largest, is just over half as wide as Pluto. The pair are sometimes called a binary system, because the centre of mass they both circle lies outside either body, and the two are tidally locked. New Horizons became the first spacecraft to visit, flying past Pluto and its moons on July 14, 2015, and taking detailed measurements.

paragraphs.heading: The search for Planet X
paragraphs.text: In the 1840s Urbain Le Verrier used Newton's laws to predict where Neptune would be, from the way it pulled on Uranus. Later observations made astronomers suspect that yet another planet was tugging on Uranus. In 1906 Percival Lowell began a large search for this ninth planet, which he called Planet X, and kept at it until he died in 1916, without success. Without anyone noticing, his own surveys had caught two faint images of Pluto in 1915.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting a moving dot
paragraphs.text: The search was handed to Clyde Tombaugh, then 23. His job was to photograph the sky in pairs of pictures and check whether anything had moved between them. With a blink comparator he flipped quickly between the two plates, so that anything that had shifted seemed to jump. On February 18, 1930, after almost a year, he found a possible moving object on plates taken on January 23 and 29. Pluto became the first known object of the Kuiper belt.

paragraphs.heading: A name from a schoolgirl
paragraphs.text: The name Pluto comes from the Roman god of the underworld, also another name for the Greek Hades. The first person to suggest it was Venetia Burney, an eleven-year-old in Oxford, England, who liked classical myths. She proposed it when her grandfather read the news at breakfast, and the idea was passed along until it was cabled to Lowell Observatory. When a vote was finally held, Pluto was the unanimous choice.

paragraphs.heading: From planet to dwarf planet
paragraphs.text: Pluto was hailed at once as the ninth planet, but doubts grew when it proved much smaller than expected. More doubts followed as other Kuiper belt objects turned up from the 1990s, above all the more massive Eris in 2005. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union (IAU) gave the word planet a formal new definition, one that leaves out dwarf planets such as Pluto. Even so, many planetary astronomers still count Pluto and other dwarf planets as planets.
